critical_code_review_comments: walkAndCollect uses recursive synchronous fs.readdirSync — fine for a postinstall context (one-shot, small node_modules subtree compared to full project). It correctly guards against permission errors with try/catch and skips .bin/.cache. No risk of infinite loops since node_modules is a DAG-like flat structure and we don't follow symlinks (fs.readdirSync default does not).
Path normalization on line 66 (`full.replace(/\\/g, '/').endsWith('/@expo/metro/metro/shared/output/bundle.js')`) correctly handles Windows backslash paths.

PATCHED_CONTENT's _try helper now strictly validates BOTH save AND build are functions — strictly correct since the downstream @expo/cli code calls `.save()` after constructing via `.build()`. This is the right invariant.

Last fallback `__dirname`-joined absolute path uses 5 levels of `..` from the shim file's location (`@expo/metro/metro/shared/output/bundle.js`), which resolves to node_modules root + `/metro/src/...`. Correct depth.
v1→v2 marker upgrade is implicit via substring match: any pre-v2 marker text (which did NOT contain the literal 'v2') gets re-patched on next run. Verified empirically. Clean upgrade semantics.

The throw on all-paths-failed (line 41-46 in PATCHED_CONTENT) gives users a clear error message instead of the cryptic original `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'save')` — improved DX even on edge-case failure.

Note: postinstall hook will be silently skipped by yarn if user passes `--ignore-scripts` or if yarn version has known scripts-skip behavior on certain lockfile-only flows. The action item for the user (already in the agent-to-agent note) is to run `node scripts/fix-metro-bundle.js` manually after `yarn install` to guarantee execution.
seed_data_creation: Temporarily downgraded v2 marker in node_modules/@expo/metro/metro/shared/output/bundle.js to the v1 string to validate the upgrade-from-v1 path, then re-ran the script which restored the v2 marker. Final on-disk state in /app: both shim files carry the v2 marker.
context_for_next_testing_agent: Iter10 v2 patch is fully verified in the cloud env. Key improvements over iter9: (1) auto-discovery via walkAndCollect replaces hardcoded paths — handles arbitrary nesting depth on the user's machine, (2) strict validation that BOTH save AND build are callable before accepting a fallback module, (3) v2 marker enables idempotent upgrade from v1. The real proof remains on the user's Windows `:app:createBundleReleaseJsAndAssets` task. If the user still hits the error, the most likely root cause is that postinstall did NOT run after their last yarn install — instruct them to run `node scripts/fix-metro-bundle.js` manually and confirm `head -1 node_modules/@expo/metro/metro/shared/output/bundle.js` shows `// Patched by scripts/fix-metro-bundle.js v2 ...`. If the file is unpatched, postinstall is being skipped (check for `--ignore-scripts`, corepack/yarn berry config, or a CI flag). If the file IS patched and the build STILL fails, ask the user to share the new stack trace — the throw inside PATCHED_CONTENT will now produce a deterministic error pinpointing which require paths were tried.
rca_of_the_issue: The recurrence after iter9 had two plausible root causes both addressed in iter10: (a) The user pulled the new repo state but did not re-run `yarn install`, so the postinstall hook never executed and their on-disk node_modules retained the original unpatched shim. (b) The user's @expo/cli structure mentioned `@expo/cli/src/...` in the trace whereas iter9 hardcoded only the `@expo/cli/build/...`-adjacent path — iter10's auto-discovery (walkAndCollect) finds shims regardless of where they live in node_modules. The strict save+build validation in _try also defends against a previously-overlooked failure mode where `metro/private/shared/output/bundle` resolves to a partial object (e.g., `{}` or build-only) on certain Node versions — iter9 only checked truthiness so a partial object could pass through and later fail when `.save()` was called; iter10 rejects partial modules and advances to the next fallback.
